claim: The mRNA levels of genes representing all three branches of UPR (spliced Xbp1 for IRE1α branch, Atf4 and Ddit3 for PERK branch, and Edem1 and Hspa5 for ATF6 branch) were up-regulated in epididymal white adipose tissues (eWAT) in C57BL/6 J mice fed high fat diet for 14 weeks.
source: In C57BL/6 J mice fed high fat diet for 14 weeks, we observed that the mRNA levels of genes representing all three branches of UPR [spliced Xbp1 (Xbp1s) for IRE1α branch, Atf4 and Ddit3 for PERK branch, and Edem1 and Hspa5 for ATF6 branch] were up-regulated in both epididymal white adipose tissues (eWAT) (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating increased mRNA levels of UPR genes in eWAT from HFD-fed mice compared to normal diet controls.

claim: The mRNA levels of genes representing all three branches of UPR were up-regulated in inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) in C57BL/6 J mice fed high fat diet for 14 weeks.
source: In C57BL/6 J mice fed high fat diet for 14 weeks, we observed that the mRNA levels of genes representing all three branches of UPR [spliced Xbp1 (Xbp1s) for IRE1α branch, Atf4 and Ddit3 for PERK branch, and Edem1 and Hspa5 for ATF6 branch] were up-regulated in both epididymal white adipose tissues (eWAT) (Figure 1A) and inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A demonstrating increased mRNA levels of UPR genes in iWAT from HFD-fed mice.

claim: Blos1 and Col6a1 mRNA levels were decreased in the eWAT of HFD-fed mice.
source: We observed that Blos1 and Col6a1 mRNA levels were decreased in the eWAT (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating decreased mRNA levels of RIDD targets Blos1 and Col6a1 in eWAT from HFD-fed mice.

claim: Col6a1 mRNA level was down-regulated in the iWAT of HFD-fed mice.
source: while Col6a1 mRNA level was also down-regulated in the iWAT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) of HFD-fed mice.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B demonstrating decreased Col6a1 mRNA levels in iWAT from HFD-fed mice.

claim: Over-nutrition/obesity triggers ER stress and IRE1α activity in adipose tissue.
source: These results suggest the over-nutrition/obesity triggers ER stress and IRE1α activity in adipose tissue.
evidence: Inferred from the observed upregulation of UPR genes and downregulation of RIDD targets in adipose tissue of HFD-fed mice.

claim: STF treatment improved glucose tolerance with lower peak glucose level and decreased AOC (area of the curve) in response to a bolus of exogenous glucose compared to vehicle-treated counterparts in DIO mice.
source: We observed that STF treatment improved glucose tolerance with lower peak glucose level and decreased AOC (area of the curve) in response to a bolus of exogenous glucose compared to their vehicle-treated counterpart (Figure 1C–C').
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 1C-C' demonstrating lower blood glucose levels and reduced area under the curve in STF-treated DIO mice.

claim: STF treatment significantly improved insulin sensitivity in DIO mice.
source: STF treatment significantly improved insulin sensitivity in DIO mice (Figure 1D–D').
evidence: Supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 1D-D' demonstrating improved insulin response in STF-treated DIO mice.

claim: STF treatment markedly decreased resting and glucose-stimulated plasma levels of insulin in DIO mice.
source: We also observed markedly decreased resting and glucose-stimulated plasma levels of insulin in DIO mice treated with STF (Figure 1E), indicative of increased insulin sensitivity in the STF-treated mice.
evidence: Supported by plasma insulin measurement data shown in Figure 1E demonstrating lower insulin levels at multiple time points after glucose injection in STF-treated mice.

claim: Insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation at Ser473 was significantly enhanced in the epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) of non-HFD lean animals.
source: Contrary to the significant enhancement in the insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation at Ser473 observed in the epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) of non-HFD lean animals, the insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation was blunted in the eWAT of DIO mice.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F-F' demonstrating increased pAKT levels in response to insulin in lean mice.

claim: Insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation was blunted in the eWAT of DIO mice.
source: Contrary to the significant enhancement in the insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation at Ser473 observed in the epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) of non-HFD lean animals, the insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation was blunted in the eWAT of DIO mice.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F-F' demonstrating reduced insulin-stimulated pAKT levels in DIO mice compared to lean controls.

claim: STF treatment significantly reversed the insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation in eWAT of DIO mice.
source: However, STF treatment significantly reversed the insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation (Figure 1F–F').
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F-F' demonstrating restored insulin-stimulated pAKT levels in STF-treated DIO mice.

claim: STF improves insulin sensitivity and glucose control under HFD.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that STF improves insulin sensitivity and glucose control under HFD.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including glucose tolerance tests, insulin tolerance tests, plasma insulin measurements, and Akt phosphorylation assays.

claim: The level of spliced Xbp1 (Xbp1s) mRNA was significantly reduced in eWAT from STF-treated DIO animals relative to vehicle group.
source: To investigate whether the STF amelioration of insulin resistance and obesity reflects on its inhibition of IRE1α activity in adipose tissue, we examined the status of IRE1α-mediated Xbp1 mRNA splicing in WAT from STF-treated DIO mice and observed that as assessed by RT-PCR followed by electrophoretic separation, the level of spliced Xbp1 (Xbp1s) mRNA was significantly reduced in both eWAT (Figure 1G–G')
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1G-G' demonstrating reduced Xbp1 splicing in eWAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: The level of spliced Xbp1 (Xbp1s) mRNA was significantly reduced in iWAT from STF-treated DIO animals relative to vehicle group.
source: the level of spliced Xbp1 (Xbp1s) mRNA was significantly reduced in both eWAT (Figure 1G–G') and iWAT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-E'') from STF-treated animals relative to vehicle group.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-E'' demonstrating reduced Xbp1 splicing in iWAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: The mRNA levels of Xbp1 target genes Hspa5 and Edem1 were highly suppressed in both eWAT and iWAT from STF-treated mice.
source: Moreover, the mRNA levels of Xbp1 target genes Hspa5 and Edem1 were highly suppressed in both eWAT and iWAT from STF-treated mice (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F demonstrating decreased expression of Hspa5 and Edem1 in adipose tissues from STF-treated mice.

claim: The mRNA levels of Atf4 and Ddit3, key components of the PERK pathway, decreased in eWAT and iWAT of STF-treated DIO mice.
source: Interestingly, we also observed the decrease in the mRNA levels of Atf4 and Ddit3, key components of the PERK pathway in eWAT and iWAT of STF-treated DIO mice (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F demonstrating decreased expression of Atf4 and Ddit3 in adipose tissues from STF-treated mice.

claim: The effect of STF treatment on PERK pathway in the adipose tissue probably reflects the positive feedback loops among the branches of UPR under in vivo conditions.
source: The effect of STF treatment on PERK pathway in the adipose tissue probably reflects the positive feedback loops among the branches of UPR under in vivo conditions as previously reported (Tsuru et al., 2013; Márton et al., 2017; Kapuy et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from observed effects on PERK pathway genes and supported by citations to previous reports of UPR crosstalk.

claim: While vehicle-treated mice continued to gain weight on HFD, 4 week STF treatment slightly decreased the body weight.
source: We observed that while vehicle-treated mice continued to gain weight on HFD, 4 week STF treatment slightly decreased the body weight (Figure 2A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A demonstrating weight reduction in STF-treated mice.

claim: There was no apparent food intake difference between the vehicle and STF groups.
source: with no apparent food intake difference between the vehicle and STF groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by food intake measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B demonstrating similar food consumption between groups.

claim: STF treatment resulted in a significant decrease in the fat mass but without significant changes in the lean mass in HFD-fed mice.
source: Body composition analysis using EchoMRI also revealed that STF treatment resulted in a significant decrease in the fat mass but without significant changes in the lean mass (Figure 2B and C) in the HFD-fed mice.
evidence: Supported by EchoMRI body composition data shown in Figure 2B and C demonstrating reduced fat mass without changes in lean mass in STF-treated mice.

claim: Adipocytes were significantly smaller from STF-treated DIO mice than that of vehicle-treated ones in both eWAT and iWAT.
source: We next analyzed the size of adipocytes in WAT sections and observed that adipocytes were significantly smaller from STF-treated DIO mice than that of vehicle-treated ones (Figure 2C and F) as shown in both average diameters (Figure 2D,G) and frequencies in large adipocytes (Figure 2E and H) in both eWAT and inguinal WAT (iWAT).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 2C-H demonstrating reduced adipocyte size in STF-treated mice.

claim: The average area of adipocytes was significantly shrunk in the eWAT and iWAT of DIO mice treated with STF relative to vehicle treatment.
source: The average area of adipocytes was similarly significantly shrunk in the eWAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and iWAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) of DIO mice treated with STF relative to vehicle treatment.
evidence: Supported by adipocyte area measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E demonstrating reduced adipocyte area in STF-treated mice.

claim: There was a significant reduction in lipid droplets in the BAT from STF-treated DIO mice.
source: In addition, there was a significant reduction in lipid droplets in the BAT from STF-treated DIO mice (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2I-J demonstrating reduced lipid droplet content in BAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: STF treatment markedly reduced the number of the lipid droplets in the liver of DIO mice compared to vehicle treatment.
source: We observed the presence of numerous lipid droplets in the liver, a hallmark of live steatosis, in the vehicle-treated DIO mice compared to that in the BL/6 mice fed normal chow (Figure 3A). Strikingly, STF treatment markedly reduced the number of the lipid droplets in the liver of DIO mice compared to vehicle treatment (Figure 3A and A').
evidence: Supported by liver histology data shown in Figure 3A-A' demonstrating reduced hepatic lipid accumulation in STF-treated mice.

claim: The lipogenic genes FASN, stearoly-coA desaturase-1 (Scd1), and acetyl coA-carboxylase (Acc) were down-regulated in the liver of STF-treated DIO mice compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: We next examined the expression of genes involved in lipogenesis in the liver of the STF- and vehicle-treated DIO mice and found that the lipogenic genes FASN, stearoly-coA desaturase-1 (Scd1), and acetyl coA-carboxylase (Acc) were down-regulated in the liver of STF-treated DIO mice compared to vehicle-treated mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B demonstrating decreased expression of lipogenic genes in liver from STF-treated mice.

claim: The expression level of G6pc1 in the liver from STF-treated DIO mice was significantly decreased compared to that of vehicle-treated ones.
source: We found that the expression level of G6pc1 in the liver from STF-treated DIO mice was also significantly decreased compared to that of vehicle-treated ones while there was no effect on Pepck expression (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C demonstrating decreased G6pc1 expression in liver from STF-treated mice.

claim: There was no effect of STF treatment on Pepck expression in the liver of DIO mice.
source: We found that the expression level of G6pc1 in the liver from STF-treated DIO mice was also significantly decreased compared to that of vehicle-treated ones while there was no effect on Pepck expression (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C demonstrating no change in Pepck expression in liver from STF-treated mice.

claim: STF treatment suppressed the macrophage accumulation of DIO mice in the liver, as marked by the F4/80 immunofluorescent staining.
source: We therefore investigated the effect of STF on macrophage population in the obese liver and observed that STF treatment suppressed the macrophage accumulation of DIO mice, as marked by the F4/80 immunofluorescent staining (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D-E demonstrating reduced F4/80-positive cells in liver from STF-treated mice.

claim: STF treatment decreased the plasma levels of triglyceride, free fatty acid (FFA), and total cholesterol.
source: Furthermore, obesity is tightly associated with dyslipidemia. We therefore examined the effect of STF on dyslipidemia and observed that STF treatment decreased the plasma levels of triglyceride, free fatty acid (FFA), and total cholesterol (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3F-H demonstrating reduced plasma lipid levels in STF-treated mice.

claim: Average oxygen consumption (VO2) was higher in DIO mice treated with STF than with vehicle.
source: We observed that average oxygen consumption (VO2) was higher in DIO mice treated with STF than with vehicle, using indirect calorimetry (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-F').
evidence: Supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-F' demonstrating increased oxygen consumption in STF-treated mice.

claim: The average carbon dioxide production (VCO2) was significantly increased in STF-treated DIO mice.
source: Similarly, the average carbon dioxide production (VCO2) was significantly increased in STF-treated DIO mice (Figure 4C–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-G').
evidence: Supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 4C-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-G' demonstrating increased carbon dioxide production in STF-treated mice.

claim: STF treatment moderately but significantly increased mean energy expenditure (EE) compared to vehicle treatment.
source: As a result, we found that STF treatment moderately but significantly increased mean (EE) compared to vehicle treatment (Figure 4E–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H-H'), without alterations in respiratory exchange ratio (RER) value or physical activities (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: Supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 4E-F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H-H' demonstrating increased energy expenditure in STF-treated mice.

claim: STF treatment did not alter respiratory exchange ratio (RER) value or physical activities.
source: As a result, we found that STF treatment moderately but significantly increased mean (EE) compared to vehicle treatment (Figure 4E–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H-H'), without alterations in respiratory exchange ratio (RER) value or physical activities (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: Supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 4G-H demonstrating no change in RER or physical activity in STF-treated mice.

claim: STF treatment reversed the whitening of BAT in DIO mice, as reflected in much less lipid droplet intensity in BAT, compared to vehicle treatment.
source: We observed that STF treatment reversed the whitening of BAT, as reflected in much less lipid droplet intensity in BAT, in DIO mice, compared to vehicle treatment (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2I demonstrating reduced lipid droplet content in BAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: STF-treated mice showed elevated staining intensity of UCP1 protein in BAT per unit area in DIO mice compared to vehicle treatment.
source: Immunofluorescent staining showed the elevated staining intensity of UCP1 protein in BAT per unit area in DIO mice compared to vehicle treatment (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I-K demonstrating increased UCP1 protein levels in BAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: STF-treated mice showed increased expression of genes involved in thermogenic and mitochondrial functions, including Prdm16, Ucp1, Cidea, Ppara, Dio2, Cox5b, and Ppargc1a (Pgc1α), in BAT.
source: Furthermore, STF-treated mice showed increased expression of genes involved in thermogenic and mitochondrial functions, including Prdm16, Ucp1, Cidea, Ppara, Dio2, Cox5b, and Ppargc1a (Pgc1α), in BAT (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4L demonstrating increased expression of thermogenic genes in BAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: STF promotes BAT activation.
source: These data thereby suggest that STF promotes BAT activation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations including reduced lipid droplets, increased UCP1 protein, and increased thermogenic gene expression in BAT.

claim: The immune-signal intensity of UCP1 protein was markedly increased in the eWAT and iWAT of DIO mice treated with STF.
source: The immune-signal intensity of UCP1 protein was markedly increased in the eWAT (Figure 4M and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) and iWAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C) of DIO mice treated with STF.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4M, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C demonstrating increased UCP1 protein levels in WAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: The expression of thermogenic genes was significantly increased in both eWAT and iWAT of DIO mice subjected to STF treatment compared to vehicle.
source: In addition, the expression of thermogenic genes was significantly increased in both eWAT and iWAT of DIO mice subjected to STF treatment compared to vehicle (Figures 4N and 3D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 4N and 3D demonstrating increased expression of thermogenic genes in WAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: STF treatment elevated the levels of both β2-adrenoceptor (Adrb2) and β3-adrenoceptor (Adrb3) in BAT.
source: Moreover, we also investigated the effect of STF on the expression -adrenoceptors, which play important role in adaptive thermogenesis in response to cold stimulation, on adipose tissues and observed that STF treatment elevated the levels of both β2-adrenoceptor (Adrb2) and β3-adrenoceptor (Adrb3) in BAT (Figure 4O)
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4O demonstrating increased expression of Adrb2 and Adrb3 in BAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: STF treatment elevated the levels of Adrb3 in iWAT and eWAT.
source: and the levels of Adrb3 in iWAT and eWAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-F').
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-F' demonstrating increased expression of Adrb3 in WAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: The area of CLS was drastically reduced in the eWAT of DIO mice treated with STF relative to vehicle-treated mice.
source: As shown in Figures 2C and 5A, the area of CLS was drastically reduced in the eWAT of DIO mice treated with STF relative to vehicle-treated mice
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figures 2C and 5A demonstrating reduced crown-like structure area in eWAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: CLS area showed no significant difference in iWAT between vehicle and STF groups.
source: although CLS area showed no significant difference in iWAT between vehicle and STF groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A demonstrating no change in crown-like structure area in iWAT between groups.

claim: Immunofluorescent staining of F4/80 was drastically increased in the eWAT under HFD, but was reversed in STF-treated mice.
source: Immunofluorescent staining of F4/80, a pan-macrophage marker, was drastically increased in the eWAT under HFD, but was reversed in STF-treated mice (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B-C demonstrating reduced F4/80-positive cells in eWAT from STF-treated mice.

claim: STF treatment significantly alleviated the mRNA levels of Cd68 and Adgre1 in the stromal vascular fraction (SVF) of the eWAT.
source: Moreover, we examined the expression levels of pan-macrophage marker genes (Cd68 and F4/80 (Adgre1)) and found that STF treatment significantly alleviated the mRNA levels of Cd68 and Adgre1 in the stromal vascular fraction (SVF where immune cells reside) of the eWAT (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D demonstrating decreased expression of macrophage marker genes in eWAT SVF from STF-treated mice.

claim: STF treatment inhibited the splicing of IRE1α target Xbp1 mRNA in the eWAT SVF.
source: Expectedly, STF treatment also inhibited the splicing of IRE1α target Xbp1 mRNA in the eWAT SVF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D demonstrating reduced Xbp1 splicing in eWAT SVF from STF-treated mice.

claim: The percentage of macrophage population (double positive for F4/80 and CD11b markers [F4/80+CD11b+]) did not alter substantially in the SVF fraction isolated from eWAT under HFD compared to normal chow.
source: We observed that the percentage of macrophage population (double positive for F4/80 and CD11b markers [F4/80+CD11b+]) did not alter substantially in the SVF fraction isolated from eWAT under HFD compared to normal chow (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A demonstrating similar percentages of F4/80+CD11b+ cells between ND and HFD groups.

claim: The total number of F4/80+CD11b+ macrophages increased drastically by 49.6-fold under HFD: 0.29±0.25 × 10^5 (normal chow, n=8) vs 1.43±0.086 × 10^6 (14-week HFD, n=8) cells/eWAT fat pad/mouse (P<0.0041).
source: however, given the HFD-induced expansion of the eWAT, the total number of F4/80+CD11b+ macrophages has increased drastically by 49.6-fold: 0.29±0.25 × 105 (normal chow, n=8) vs 1.43±0.086 × 106 (14-week HFD, n=8) cells/eWAT fat pad/mouse (Pp0.0041) (Table 1a).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification data shown in Table 1a demonstrating increased total ATM numbers in HFD-fed mice.

claim: The density of F4/80+CD11b+ macrophage population in eWAT increased under HFD by 12.5-fold after normalizing the total number of macrophages to fat pad weight (0.62±0.45 × 10^5 (normal chow) vs. 0.77±0.015 × 10^6 cells (14 week HFD)/g of eWAT/mouse, p=0.0045).
source: The density of F4/80+CD11b+ macrophage population in eWAT also increased under HFD by 12.5-fold after normalizing the total number of macrophages to fat pad weight (0.62±0.45 × 105 (normal chow) vs. 0.77±0.015 × 106 cells (14 week HFD)/g of eWAT/mouse, p=0.0045, Table 1a).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification data shown in Table 1a demonstrating increased ATM density in HFD-fed mice.

claim: STF treatment significantly lessened the HFD-induced increases in the percentage, total number, and density of ATMs by 37.4%, 46%, and 54%, respectively.
source: Excitingly, STF treatment significantly lessened the HFD-induced increases in the percentage, total number, and density of ATMs by 37.4%, 46%, and 54%, respectively (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and Table 1a).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification data shown in Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, and Table 1a demonstrating reduced ATM accumulation in STF-treated mice.

claim: STF suppresses macrophage accumulation in the adipose tissue.
source: These results indicate that STF suppresses macrophage accumulation in the adipose tissue.
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations including reduced CLS area, F4/80 staining, macrophage marker gene expression, and flow cytometry quantification of ATMs.

claim: Under HFD, the percentage of F4/80+CD11b+CD11c+ triple positive cells was markedly increased in the eWAT (14.59% (ND) vs. 52.95% (HFD), p=0.007).
source: We observed that under HFD, the percentage (14.59% (ND) vs. 52.95% (HFD), p=0.007, Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, Table 1b), total number/eWAT/mouse (0.25±0.16 × 104 (ND, n=8) vs 0.75±0.11 × 106 (HFD, n=8), 299.58-fold, p<0.0001, Table 1b), and density/g of eWAT/mouse (0.59±0.23 x 104 (ND) vs. 4.11±0.96 x 105 (HFD), 70-fold, p=0.0018, Table 1b) of F4/80+CD11b+CD11c+ triple positive cells, which are typically characterized as the classical 'M1-like' adipose tissue macrophages, were markedly increased in the eWAT.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, and Table 1b demonstrating increased CD11c+ ATM percentage in HFD-fed mice.

claim: Under HFD, the total number of F4/80+CD11b+CD11c+ triple positive cells per eWAT per mouse was markedly increased (0.25±0.16 × 10^4 (ND, n=8) vs 0.75±0.11 × 10^6 (HFD, n=8), 299.58-fold, p<0.0001).
source: We observed that under HFD, the percentage (14.59% (ND) vs. 52.95% (HFD), p=0.007, Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, Table 1b), total number/eWAT/mouse (0.25±0.16 × 104 (ND, n=8) vs 0.75±0.11 × 106 (HFD, n=8), 299.58-fold, p<0.0001, Table 1b), and density/g of eWAT/mouse (0.59±0.23 x 104 (ND) vs. 4.11±0.96 x 105 (HFD), 70-fold, p=0.0018, Table 1b) of F4/80+CD11b+CD11c+ triple positive cells, which are typically characterized as the classical 'M1-like' adipose tissue macrophages, were markedly increased in the eWAT.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification data shown in Table 1b demonstrating increased total CD11c+ ATM numbers in HFD-fed mice.

claim: Under HFD, the density of F4/80+CD11b+CD11c+ triple positive cells per g of eWAT per mouse was markedly increased (0.59±0.23 x 10^4 (ND) vs. 4.11±0.96 x 10^5 (HFD), 70-fold, p=0.0018).
source: We observed that under HFD, the percentage (14.59% (ND) vs. 52.95% (HFD), p=0.007, Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, Table 1b), total number/eWAT/mouse (0.25±0.16 × 104 (ND, n=8) vs 0.75±0.11 × 106 (HFD, n=8), 299.58-fold, p<0.0001, Table 1b), and density/g of eWAT/mouse (0.59±0.23 x 104 (ND) vs. 4.11±0.96 x 105 (HFD), 70-fold, p=0.0018, Table 1b) of F4/80+CD11b+CD11c+ triple positive cells, which are typically characterized as the classical 'M1-like' adipose tissue macrophages, were markedly increased in the eWAT.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification data shown in Table 1b demonstrating increased CD11c+ ATM density in HFD-fed mice.

claim: The bulk majority of CD11c+ ATMs were also positive for CD206 in the eWAT under HFD.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that the bulk majority of these CD11c+ ATMs were also positive for CD206, a marker thought for M2 macrophages, in the eWAT under HFD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B demonstrating CD206 expression in CD11c+ ATMs.

claim: Approximately half the population is positive for both CD11c and CD206 in DIO ATMs, whereas there are only 8.55% CD11c+CD206+ ATMs under ND when gated against CD11c and CD206.
source: and that approximately half the population is positive for both CD11c and CD206 in DIO ATMs, whereas there are only 8.55% CD11c+CD206+ ATMs under ND when gated against CD11c and CD206 (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A demonstrating increased CD11c+CD206+ ATMs in HFD-fed mice.

claim: The total number and density of CD11c+CD206+ ATMs increased by 337- and 75-fold respectively under HFD.
source: Moreover, we found that the total number and density of CD11c+CD206+ ATMs increased by 337- and 75-fold respectively under HFD (Table 1c; ND: n=8; HFD: n=8), a greater increase than those of CD11C-postive alone (CD11c+CD206-) ATMs under HFD (Supplementary file 1; ND: n=8; HFD: n=8).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification data shown in Table 1c demonstrating increased CD11c+CD206+ ATM numbers and density in HFD-fed mice.

claim: For CD206+CD11c- ATM subpopulation, HFD drove the increase in the total cell number and density of this population by over 16- and 4-fold respectively despite the diminished percentage given the huge expansion of total ATMs.
source: On the other hand, for CD206+CD11c- ATM subpopulation, a presumed M2-like ATM subpopulation which accounted for the majority of ATMs under ND as expected (Figure 5G and Table 1d), HFD drove the increase in the total cell number and density of this population by over 16- and 4-fold respectively despite the diminished percentage given the huge expansion of total ATMs (Table 1d; ND: n=8; HFD: n=8), although to a lesser degree than that for CD11c+CD206+ or CD11c+CD206- macrophages (Table 1c and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification data shown in Table 1d demonstrating increased CD206+CD11c- ATM numbers and density in HFD-fed mice.

claim: CD206-CD11c- ATM subpopulation exhibited a trend similar to that of CD206+CD11c- ATMs.
source: Moreover, CD206-CD11c- ATM subpopulation also exhibited a trend similar to that of CD206+CD11c- ATMs (Supplementary file 1b; ND: n=8; HFD: n=8).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification data shown in Supplementary file 1b demonstrating changes in CD206-CD11c- ATMs in HFD-fed mice.

claim: ATMs do not follow the classic M2 to M1 switch.
source: Our findings confirm the notion that ATMs do not follow the classic M2 to M1 switch (Xu et al., 2013; Kratz et al., 2014; Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from observations of mixed M1/M2 phenotypes and supported by citations to previous studies.

evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C demonstrating decreased expression of proinflammatory genes in iWAT SVF from STF-treated mice.

claim: The RNase activity of ER stress sensor IRE1α is up-regulated in the adipose tissue of mice with diet-induced obesity.

claim: The increased IRE1α activity precedes the onset of diabetes in the mice with obesity.
source: and that the increased IRE1α activity precedes the onset of diabetes in the mice with obesity.

claim: The inhibition of IRE1α activity is able to reverse HFD-induced insulin resistance and comorbidities.

claim: The increased IRE1α activity is an important contributor to obesity-associated insulin resistance.

evidence: Inferred from the observation that inhibiting IRE1α reverses insulin resistance in obese mice.

claim: STF promotes thermogenesis and energy expenditure and counters diet-induced obesity.
source: We showed that STF promotes thermogenesis and energy expenditure and counters diet-induced obesity.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased energy expenditure, UCP1 expression, thermogenic gene expression, and reduced body weight in STF-treated mice.

claim: The IRE1α inhibition by STF suppresses the accumulation of proinflammatory ATMs, including previously identified CD11c+ ATMs and the recently identified CD9+ ATMs, and adipose inflammation.

evidence: Supported by data showing reduced ATM populations and decreased proinflammatory gene expression in adipose tissue of STF-treated mice.

claim: The CD11c+ ATMs are largely overlapping with but yet non-identical to CD9+ ATMs in the eWAT under HFD.

evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing high but incomplete overlap between CD11c and CD9 expression in ATMs.

claim: The suppression of ATM population/inflammation by STF inhibition of IRE1α is associated with the reversal of the obesity-suppressed expression of thermogenic/mitochondrial oxidation genes in adipose tissue to promote thermogenesis.

evidence: Inferred from observations of reduced ATM inflammation and increased thermogenic gene expression in STF-treated mice, supported by citations to previous studies on inflammation-mediated suppression of thermogenesis.

claim: Macrophage-derived proinflammatory cytokines such as TNFα and IL1b directly suppress the induction of Ucp1 expression in adipocytes and impair cold-induced thermogenesis in rodents.

evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating the suppressive effects of proinflammatory cytokines on thermogenesis.

claim: HFD-induced obesity and chronic adipose inflammation are associated with the reduced expression of thermogenic/mitochondrial oxidation genes and the repression of thermogenesis.

evidence: Supported by citation to previous study demonstrating association between obesity/inflammation and reduced thermogenesis.
